micro.title: Day 1 — one pass, a few variables, and writing in place

sections.title: Today in one minute
sections.body:
Day 1 is about **not looking back**. Two ideas, four easy problems, and the habits you will use for the next 29 days.

✍️ **Running state** — walk once, keep a few variables that summarise the past.
✍️ **Read/write pointer** — one index reads everything, another marks where the next kept element goes.

The reading path below takes about 20 minutes (longer than usual — it includes the foundations). Every page opens inside the path; when you finish a step you continue from here.

sections.title: Pattern card
sections.body:
✍️ RUNNING STATE — trigger: "so far / running / streak / consecutive". Keep: total, current, best. Update every step; reset when the condition breaks.
✍️ READ/WRITE POINTER — trigger: "in-place", "O(1) extra space", "remove/move, keep order". `if keep(a[read]) a[write++] = a[read]`. Return `write`.

drill.title: Find Numbers with Even Number of Digits
drill.statement: Given a list of positive integers, count how many of them are written with an even number of decimal digits.
drill.approach: One pass; for each number count its digits (divide by 10, or check ranges 10–99, 1000–9999, …) and increment a counter if the count is even.
drill.trigger: "count how many elements satisfy …" with an independent per-element test.
drill.details:
**Task.** You get an array of positive integers. Count the numbers whose decimal representation has an even number of digits.

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 500; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[12, 345, 2, 6, 7896]` → `2`. 12 has two digits and 7896 has four; the others have an odd count.

drill.title: Richest Customer Wealth
drill.statement: A grid lists, for each customer (row), the money they hold in each bank (column). Return the largest total wealth of any single customer.
drill.pattern_name: Running sum per row + best so far
drill.approach: For each row, sum it with a running total, then update a global maximum.
drill.details:
**Task.** An m × n grid `accounts` gives, for customer i (a row), the amount they keep in bank j (a column). A customer's wealth is the total across all their banks. Return the wealth of the richest customer.

**Input:** a 2-D integer array. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 50; 1 ≤ `accounts[i][j]` ≤ 100.

**Example:** `[[1,5],[7,3],[3,5]]` → `10`. The totals are 6, 10 and 8.

drill.title: Element Appearing More Than 25% In Sorted Array
drill.statement: A sorted array has exactly one value that occurs in more than a quarter of the positions. Return it.
drill.approach: Duplicates are adjacent in sorted input, so track the length of the current run of equal values and return the value when the run exceeds n/4. (Clever version: check if a[i] == a[i + n/4].)
drill.trigger: "sorted" + "appears more than …" → equal values sit together, count runs.
drill.details:
**Task.** An array sorted in non-decreasing order contains exactly one value that fills more than 25% of its positions. Return that value.

**Input:** a sorted integer array `arr`. **Output:** an integer.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 10⁴; 0 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 10⁵.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 2, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 10]` → `6`. It fills 4 of the 9 positions, which is more than a quarter.

drill.title: Three Consecutive Odds
drill.statement: Return true if the array contains three odd numbers in a row.
drill.approach: Streak counter that increments on odd and resets on even; return true when it reaches 3.
drill.details:
**Task.** Return true if somewhere in the array there are three odd numbers at consecutive positions, otherwise false.

**Input:** an integer array `arr`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 1 ≤ length ≤ 1000; 1 ≤ `arr[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 34, 3, 4, 5, 7, 23, 12]` → `true` (5, 7, 23). `[2, 6, 4, 1]` → `false`.

drill.title: Remove One Element to Make the Array Strictly Increasing
drill.statement: Decide whether deleting exactly one element can leave the array strictly increasing.
drill.approach: Walk once counting positions where a[i] ≤ a[i−1]. More than one → false. At the single violation, check whether removing a[i−1] or a[i] fixes it by comparing with a[i−2] / a[i+1].
drill.trigger: "remove one element" + "strictly increasing" → scan once for the violation, decide locally.
drill.details:
**Task.** Remove exactly one element from the array. Can the remaining elements, in their original order, be strictly increasing? (An array that is already strictly increasing also counts: removing any one element keeps it so.)

**Input:** an integer array `nums`. **Output:** a boolean.

**Constraints:** 2 ≤ length ≤ 1000; 1 ≤ `nums[i]` ≤ 1000.

**Example:** `[1, 2, 10, 5, 7]` → `true`: remove 10 to get `[1, 2, 5, 7]`. `[2, 3, 1, 2]` → `false`. `[1, 1, 1]` → `false`.

core.subject: OOP
core.title: Classes, objects and their memory · Constructors and destructors
core.explain: An interviewer asks: "What exactly happens in memory when you write `Account a(100);` and when `a` goes out of scope?" Answer in 2 minutes: object layout, constructor call, stack vs heap, destructor call.

intro.title: Today
intro.body:
OOP is the first CS subject because every LLD round and many C++ questions sit on top of it. Today: what an object actually is in memory, and how it is born and destroyed.
✍️ Read topic 1 → write its note → answer its recall questions. Then topic 2. Then the MCQs and the 2-minute explanation.

mcqs.q: In C++, what is the only difference between `struct` and `class`?

options.b: struct members and base classes are public by default; class ones are private
options.c: struct objects live on the stack, class objects on the heap

mcqs.why: Both can have functions, constructors, inheritance and live anywhere. Only the default access differs.

mcqs.q: `class A { char c; int x; };` — on a typical 64-bit compiler, `sizeof(A)` is most likely:
mcqs.why: 1 byte for c, 3 bytes of padding so the int is 4-byte aligned, 4 bytes for x → 8.

mcqs.q: What does `sizeof` of a class with no data members return?
mcqs.why: Every object must have a distinct address, so an empty class has size 1.

mcqs.q: In which order are members initialised?

options.a: The order they appear in the initialiser list
options.c: The order they are declared in the class

mcqs.why: Declaration order always wins; compilers warn (-Wreorder) when the initialiser list order differs.

mcqs.q: `Derived` inherits from `Base`. Creating and destroying a `Derived` object calls, in order:
mcqs.why: Construction goes base → derived; destruction is the exact reverse.

mcqs.q: Which members MUST be set in the constructor initialiser list (not in the body)?
mcqs.why: const and reference members cannot be assigned after construction, so they must be initialised in the list.

reading_path.bridge: Every problem in this plan starts with this box on paper. Read it once — you will fill it four times today.
How a slow solution becomes a fast one. Today's problems are the gentlest examples of this method.
The five-slot pseudocode you write on paper before any C++.
Just enough Big-O to say "this is O(n)" and mean it.
The container in every problem. Note the size() trap.
Pattern 1 of today: carry the past in a few variables. Used by problems 1 and 2.
Pattern 2 of today: compacting an array in place. Used by problems 3 and 4.
